title: Consider the Lobster
author: David Foster Wallace
blurb: The Maine Lobster Festival, and whether boiling a lobster alive is defensible. Assigned as festival coverage; delivered as an argument about pain.

title: Roger Federer as Religious Experience
author: David Foster Wallace
blurb: The 2006 Wimbledon final, and what a human body does at the limit of what bodies do.

title: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?
author: Thomas Nagel
blurb: Whether the subjective character of experience can be captured by any physical description of the brain.

title: Once More to the Lake
author: E. B. White
blurb: White takes his son to the Maine lake he went to as a child and cannot keep the two visits separate.

title: On Self-Respect
author: Joan Didion
blurb: What it costs to be responsible for your own life, written after Didion was not admitted to Phi Beta Kappa.

title: Goodbye to All That
author: Joan Didion
blurb: Eight years in New York, from arriving at twenty to leaving at twenty-eight.

title: Notes on "Camp"
author: Susan Sontag
blurb: A sensibility that prefers artifice, exaggeration, and failed seriousness, catalogued rather than argued.

title: The Inner Ring
author: C. S. Lewis
blurb: The desire to be inside the group that matters, and why that desire never resolves.

title: Shooting an Elephant
author: George Orwell
blurb: A colonial police officer in Burma shoots an elephant he does not want to shoot because a crowd expects it.

title: Politics and the English Language
author: George Orwell
blurb: How vague, prefabricated prose makes indefensible political positions defensible.

title: Self-Reliance
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
blurb: Conformity as the standing threat to a person's actual judgment.

title: Street Haunting: A London Adventure
author: Virginia Woolf
blurb: Walking across London at dusk on the excuse of buying a pencil, and what the self does when it is unobserved.

title: The Death of the Moth
author: Virginia Woolf
blurb: Woolf watches a moth die on a windowpane over the course of an afternoon.

title: Notes of a Native Son
author: James Baldwin
blurb: His father's funeral, which fell on Baldwin's nineteenth birthday and the day the 1943 Harlem riot began.

title: How It Feels to Be Colored Me
author: Zora Neale Hurston
blurb: Hurston on becoming "colored" at thirteen when she left an all-Black town for Jacksonville, and refusing the tragic register afterward.

title: Total Eclipse
author: Annie Dillard
blurb: The February 26, 1979 total solar eclipse, seen from a hillside in central Washington State.

title: The Median Isn't the Message
author: Stephen Jay Gould
blurb: Gould is diagnosed with abdominal mesothelioma, reads that median survival is eight months, and works out what the distribution actually means.

title: The Opposite of Loneliness
author: Marina Keegan
blurb: What college gave her that has no single word for it, and the argument that it is not too late for anything.

title: On Bullshit
author: Harry G. Frankfurt
blurb: The formal difference between a liar, who tracks the truth in order to avoid it, and a bullshitter, who is indifferent to it.

title: Men Explain Things to Me
author: Rebecca Solnit
blurb: A man at a party explains a book to Solnit at length. The book is hers.

title: On Keeping a Notebook
author: Joan Didion
blurb: Why she writes things down, and the fact that her notebooks record almost nothing that actually happened.

title: A Hanging
author: George Orwell
blurb: An execution in a Burmese jail, and the prisoner stepping around a puddle on the way to the gallows.

title: On Being Ill
author: Virginia Woolf
blurb: Why literature has almost nothing to say about being sick, which is one of the most common human states.

title: Stranger in the Village
author: James Baldwin
blurb: Baldwin spends a winter in a Swiss alpine village where no Black person has ever been, and works out what that says about America rather than Switzerland.

title: Death of a Pig
author: E. B. White
blurb: White tries and fails to save a sick pig he had bought to slaughter.

title: The Absurd
author: Thomas Nagel
blurb: Why life feels absurd, argued as a collision between how seriously we take our own lives and the view from outside them.

title: Epiphenomenal Qualia
author: Frank Jackson
blurb: Mary knows every physical fact about color vision but has only seen black and white. What happens when she leaves the room.

title: Regarding the Torture of Others
author: Susan Sontag
blurb: The Abu Ghraib photographs, and the argument that the pictures are not evidence of what happened but part of what happened.

title: Why Are Americans Afraid of Dragons?
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
blurb: Why American adults treat imaginative fiction as frivolous, and what that costs.

title: Meditation in a Toolshed
author: C. S. Lewis
blurb: The difference between looking *at* a beam of light and standing in it looking *along* it, applied to every kind of knowledge.

title: In Search of Zora Neale Hurston
author: Alice Walker
blurb: Walker goes to Fort Pierce, Florida, posing as Hurston's niece, to find her unmarked grave.

title: The White Negro: Superficial Reflections on the Hipster
author: Norman Mailer
blurb: Mailer's theory of the white hipster who adopts what he takes to be Black existential freedom.

title: Lying in Politics: Reflections on The Pentagon Papers
author: Hannah Arendt
blurb: Written weeks after the Pentagon Papers were published. How a government's "problem-solvers" replaced facts with models and then believed the models.

title: A Few Words About Breasts
author: Nora Ephron
blurb: Ephron on having small breasts, and on the fact that this genuinely determined her adolescence.

title: ChatGPT Is a Blurry JPEG of the Web
author: Ted Chiang
blurb: Large language models as lossy compression of their training data, with fluency filling in what was discarded.

title: Mother F—er
author: Emily Ratajkowski
blurb: After her divorce she dated compulsively, not to find a partner but to test whether she was still desirable as a mother, and adopted a deliberate villain persona while doing it.

title: Buying Myself Back: When Does a Model Own Her Own Image?
author: Emily Ratajkowski
blurb: Four episodes in which other people owned, sold, or sued over images of her body — a photographer, Richard Prince, a paparazzo, and an ex.

title: The Crane Wife
author: CJ Hauser
blurb: Ten days after calling off her wedding, Hauser joins a whooping crane research expedition in Texas, and uses the Japanese folktale of the crane wife to describe having trained herself to need nothing.

title: What Do We Do with the Art of Monstrous Men?
author: Claire Dederer
blurb: Whether you can keep loving the work of Woody Allen, Polanski, and Cosby, and why "separate the art from the artist" does not function as an answer.

title: The Age of Instagram Face
author: Jia Tolentino
blurb: How FaceTune, filters, and injectables converged on one globally identical, ethnically ambiguous face.

title: AI has a sex addiction
author: Millie Hughes
blurb: Three linked claims — that web-scraped training corpora are saturated with pornography (cites the Google Imagen audit, the ~3,200 CSAM images found in LAION, allegations about Meta); that porn's racialized conventions, specifically the submissive East and Southeast Asian woman, propagate into model output; and that this produces measurable harm, using the Equinox ad featuring a dismembered AI-generated Asian woman as the case study.

title: The Goon Squad
author: Daniel Kolitz
blurb: Gooning — extended edging aimed at a dissociative "goonstate" — as a Gen Z online subculture, framed as a symptom of social breakdown. Opens on the January suicide of Nautica Malone after a viral indecent-exposure video.

title: Elon Musk and the Infinite Rebuy
author: Dave Karpf
blurb: A poker metaphor applied to Isaacson's Musk biography. In a tournament with unlimited rebuys, the player with infinite money eventually wins. "You just need access to enough money to keep rebuying until you succeed."

title: Universal Love, Said The Cactus Person — FICTION, recommend cutting
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: # PART 4 — 14 more in that lane

title: The Web Is a Customer Service Medium
author: Paul Ford
blurb: The web is not a publishing medium but a customer service medium, because its fundamental driver is "Why wasn't I consulted?"

title: The Artificial Intelligence Revolution: Part 1
author: Tim Urban
blurb: Exponential progress puts AGI and then superintelligence far closer than intuition suggests.

title: Superintelligence: The Idea That Eats Smart People
author: Maciej Cegłowski
blurb: Dismantles Bostrom-style AI doom premise by premise, and argues the belief functions as status religion for tech elites while distracting from present-day AI harms.

title: The Premium Mediocre Life of Maya Millennial
author: Venkatesh Rao
blurb: "Premium mediocre" — truffle oil, Starbucks sizing, Instagrammable everything — as self-aware class performance by precarious young professionals, not naive aspiration.

title: Silicon Valley Is Turning Into Its Own Worst Fear
author: Ted Chiang
blurb: The paperclip-maximizer AI Silicon Valley fears already exists. It is the corporation, and the fear is unacknowledged self-portraiture.

title: Everyone Is Beautiful and No One Is Horny
author: R. S. Benedict
blurb: Blockbuster cinema fetishizes optimized bodies while stripping them of desire — bodies as military and labor assets rather than sites of pleasure.

title: standing on the shoulders of complex female characters
author: Rayne Fisher-Quann
blurb: Young women assemble identity and suffering as curated consumption, so pain becomes an aesthetic commodity indistinguishable from performance.

title: Tiktok's enshittification
author: Cory Doctorow
blurb: Platforms die in a fixed three-stage sequence — good to users, then abusive to users in favor of business customers, then abusive to everyone to claw back all value.

title: Effective obfuscation
author: Molly White
blurb: Effective altruism and effective accelerationism are the same product in different packaging — philosophies that let wealthy technologists describe self-enrichment as service to humanity.

title: The State of the Culture, 2024
author: Ted Gioia
blurb: Art and entertainment are both being displaced by a fourth category — engineered distraction — producing a dopamine culture whose endpoint is anhedonia.

title: I Will Fucking Piledrive You If You Mention AI Again
author: Nikhil Suresh
blurb: The enterprise AI boom is executives cosplaying strategy at organizations that cannot manage a spreadsheet, and the actual work is unglamorous data hygiene.

title: What is "slop," exactly?
author: Max Read
blurb: Slop is not defined by AI production but by consumption conditions — anything optimized to frictionlessness until it loses individuation. "Netflix slop," "carslop."

title: Meditations On Moloch
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: Coordination failures — multipolar traps, personified as Ginsberg's Moloch — as the root cause of most systemic misery.

title: The rise and fall of peer review
author: Adam Mastroianni
blurb: Peer review is a recent invention, not a timeless feature of science, and the evidence that it improves papers is thin.

title: A Modest Proposal
author: Jonathan Swift
blurb: A deadpan projector proposes the Irish poor sell their one-year-olds as food to English landlords, with costings and cooking suggestions.

title: Fenimore Cooper's Literary Offences
author: Mark Twain
blurb: Twain lays out 18 rules of romantic fiction and demolishes Cooper for breaking all of them, counting "114 offences against literary art out of a possible 115" in two-thirds of a page of *The Deerslayer*.

title: Letter to Lord Chesterfield
author: Samuel Johnson
blurb: Chesterfield ignored Johnson for the seven years he wrote the *Dictionary*, then published puffs for it just before publication. Johnson declines.

title: On the Knocking at the Gate in Macbeth
author: Thomas De Quincey
blurb: Why the knocking right after Duncan's murder produces such a jolt — it marks the moment the ordinary world restarts, retroactively showing how far Macbeth's world had gone.

title: Of Studies
author: Francis Bacon
blurb: What reading is for. "Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested."

title: Of Cannibals
author: Michel de Montaigne
blurb: Montaigne interviews Brazilians brought to Rouen, describes Tupinambá ritual cannibalism, and argues Europeans who torture and burn people alive are the greater barbarians.

title: On the Shortness of Life (De Brevitate Vitae)
author: Seneca
blurb: Life is not short; people squander it on status, busywork, and other people's business.

title: The Spectator No. 26 (Reflections in Westminster Abbey)
author: Joseph Addison
blurb: Addison walks among the tombs and epitaphs and turns it into a meditation on death and the absurdity of monuments.

title: A Dissertation Upon Roast Pig
author: Charles Lamb
blurb: A mock-scholarly origin myth in which roast pork is discovered in China when a boy burns down a house with piglets inside, followed by a rhapsody on crackling.

title: On the Pleasure of Hating
author: William Hazlitt
blurb: Starting from a spider on his floor, Hazlitt argues malice is a positive appetite rather than a failure of virtue — that we need enemies, enjoy public hatreds, and eventually turn on our friends and our own past selves.

title: Civil Disobedience
author: Henry David Thoreau
blurb: Thoreau refuses to pay a poll tax funding slavery and the Mexican–American War, spends a night in jail, and argues a just individual withdraws support from an unjust state rather than waiting for majorities.

title: Ain't I a Woman?
author: Sojourner Truth
blurb: Truth tells a white women's convention that the chivalry claimed as women's nature was never extended to her.

title: What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?
author: Frederick Douglass
blurb: Douglass praises the founders at length, then pivots to tell a white audience that Independence Day is, to the enslaved, "a thin veil to cover up crimes which would disgrace a nation of savages."

title: The Soul of Man Under Socialism
author: Oscar Wilde
blurb: Socialism's real value is not equality but the abolition of drudgery, freeing everyone for individualism and art. Charity, Wilde argues, is part of the disease.

title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine
blurb: A plain-language case that hereditary monarchy is absurd, reconciliation with Britain is impossible, and America should declare independence now.

title: Self-Reliance
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
blurb: Duplicate cross-reference to #11; kept so the pre-1900 group reads as a complete run.

title: Of Our Spiritual Strivings
author: W. E. B. Du Bois
blurb: What it is to live as a problem in America.

title: Modern Fiction
author: Virginia Woolf
blurb: The Edwardian "materialists" — Bennett, Wells, Galsworthy — describe the body of life and miss the mind.

title: On Being the Right Size
author: J. B. S. Haldane
blurb: The square-cube law applied to biology. A mouse dropped down a mine shaft walks away; a horse splashes. Insects breathe by diffusion because they are small.

title: Letter from Birmingham Jail
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
blurb: Why the white moderate's call for patience is a greater obstacle than the Klan, and when disobeying a law is a moral duty.

title: Letter from a Region in My Mind
author: James Baldwin
blurb: Baldwin's teenage pentecostalism, a dinner with Elijah Muhammad, and the psychology of American whiteness.

title: The Master's Tools Will Never Dismantle the Master's House
author: Audre Lorde
blurb: A Black lesbian invited as the panel's only non-white voice tells the organizers that the format is the problem.

title: Frank Sinatra Has a Cold
author: Gay Talese
blurb: A profile of Sinatra built entirely from observation, after Sinatra refused to be interviewed.

title: The Kentucky Derby Is Decadent and Depraved
author: Hunter S. Thompson
blurb: Thompson and Steadman fail to cover the Derby and cover the crowd, and themselves, instead.

title: Radical Chic: That Party at Lenny's
author: Tom Wolfe
blurb: Leonard Bernstein's January 14, 1970 Park Avenue fundraiser for the Black Panther 21.

title: The White Album
author: Joan Didion
blurb: Didion's psychiatric report, the Manson murders, Huey Newton, and the collapse of narrative in late-1960s Los Angeles.

title: As We May Think
author: Vannevar Bush
blurb: Written as the war ends, argues the real postwar problem is the unmanageable growth of the scientific record, and proposes the "memex" — a desk that stores documents on microfilm and lets a user build permanent associative trails between them.

title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
author: Alan Turing
blurb: Replaces "Can machines think?" with the imitation game, then answers nine objections including the theological one and Lady Lovelace's.

title: Cargo Cult Science
author: Richard Feynman
blurb: Research that follows all the outward forms of science and produces nothing, with Millikan's oil-drop constant drifting slowly toward the true value as the case study in how scientists deceive themselves.

title: The Tragedy of the Commons — include the criticism with it
author: Garrett Hardin
blurb: A resource open to all is destroyed, because each user gains the full benefit of one more animal while the cost of overgrazing is shared. Hardin's remedy is "mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon," applied above all to human reproduction.

title: Thinking Like a Mountain
author: Aldo Leopold
blurb: Leopold shoots a wolf, watches "a fierce green fire dying in her eyes," and follows the consequence — deer irruption, then a mountain stripped bare.

title: The man who mistook his wife for a hat
author: Oliver Sacks
blurb: A musician with visual agnosia can describe every feature of an object but cannot recognize the whole, and navigates only by singing.

title: The Iliad, or the Poem of Force
author: Simone Weil
blurb: Reads the *Iliad* as a poem whose real protagonist is force — "that x that turns anybody who is subjected to it into a thing" — and insists it degrades the one who wields it as surely as the one it destroys.

title: The Myth of Sisyphus — the final chapter
author: Albert Camus
blurb: Sisyphus is the absurd hero because he is fully conscious of the futility of his punishment. The descent back down the mountain, not the pushing, is where he becomes free of it.

title: Kafka and His Precursors
author: Jorge Luis Borges
blurb: Assembles six texts with nothing in common — Zeno's paradox, a Han Yu allegory, Kierkegaard, Browning, Léon Bloy, Lord Dunsany — and shows each becomes Kafkaesque only once Kafka exists.

title: Why Read the Classics?
author: Italo Calvino
blurb: Fourteen successive definitions of a classic, including "a book that has never finished saying what it has to say" and the deflationary "a book which people praise and don't read."

title: The Storyteller: Reflections on the Works of Nikolai Leskov
author: Walter Benjamin
blurb: Storytelling is dying because experience has become uncommunicable — soldiers came back from the trenches silent — and the novel, and worse, *information*, have replaced the story.

title: The Gray Zone
author: Primo Levi
blurb: The *Sonderkommando*, and the collapse of a clean line between victim and perpetrator inside the camp.

title: Ur-Fascism
author: Umberto Eco
blurb: Fourteen overlapping features of "Eternal Fascism," presented as a Wittgensteinian family resemblance rather than a definition.

title: E Unibus Pluram: Television and U.S. Fiction
author: David Foster Wallace
blurb: How television absorbed irony as its own defense, and why that leaves American fiction disarmed.

title: The Fourth State of Matter
author: Jo Ann Beard
blurb: Beard, then an editor in the University of Iowa physics and astronomy department, braids a collapsing marriage and a dying dog with the November 1, 1991 campus shooting in which grad student Gang Lu killed five people, including her close friend Christoph Goertz.

title: The Naked Citadel
author: Susan Faludi
blurb: Inside The Citadel, South Carolina's all-male state military college — the hazing culture, the sexual pathology, and the institutional defense mobilized against admitting women.

title: The Search for Marvin Gardens
author: John McPhee
blurb: A Monopoly game intercut with a walk through the actual decayed Atlantic City streets the board names.

title: Undersea
author: Rachel Carson
blurb: The ocean narrated from the point of view of its inhabitants rather than a human observer, from shore to abyssal plain.

title: The Lives of a Cell
author: Lewis Thomas
blurb: We are not single organisms but colonies — mitochondria and chloroplasts as descendants of captured bacteria, so "my cells are no longer the pure line entities I was raised with."

title: The Tragedy of Central Europe
author: Milan Kundera
blurb: Central Europe is culturally Western and politically Eastern, and its absorption by Russia is a European catastrophe Europe has not noticed.

title: In Praise of Shadows
author: Jun'ichirō Tanizaki
blurb: An aesthetic built on shadow, patina, and dimness — lacquerware made for candlelight, gold leaf that glows only in gloom, No theater, the toilet as a place of contemplation — against the flattening glare of Western electric light.

title: Shame
author: Primo Levi
blurb: Why survivors felt shame rather than relief at liberation — shame at having survived in place of someone better, at not having resisted, at belonging to the species that built the camp.

title: The Sons of La Malinche
author: Octavio Paz
blurb: *La Chingada* — Malinche as violated mother, and Mexicans as *hijos de la chingada*, sons of the violation.

title: The Black Boy Looks at the White Boy
author: James Baldwin
blurb: Baldwin's friendship and rivalry with Norman Mailer, and his refusal of Mailer's hipster-as-Negro romance.

title: The Last American Hero Is Junior Johnson. Yes!
author: Tom Wolfe
blurb: Moonshine-runner-turned-NASCAR-driver Junior Johnson in Wilkes County, North Carolina.

title: Hell Sucks / Khe Sanh
author: Michael Herr
blurb: "Hell Sucks" is the Battle of Huế during the Tet Offensive; "Khe Sanh" is the 1968 siege.

title: Grand Unified Theory of Female Pain
author: Leslie Jamison
blurb: Why depictions of wounded women get dismissed as cliché, and whether that dismissal is itself a way of not taking women's pain seriously.

title: The Argentine Writer and Tradition
author: Jorge Luis Borges
blurb: Rejects the demand that Argentine writers use local colour, noting the *Koran* contains no camels; argues peripheral writers can handle all of Western culture with more freedom than its inheritors, as Jews and Irishmen have done.

title: Encountering the Other: The Challenge for the 21st Century
author: Ryszard Kapuściński
blurb: The encounter with the Other as the defining ethical problem of the century, argued through Herodotus, Lévinas, and Buber against Europe's habit of treating the Other as object.

title: The Fine Art of Baloney Detection
author: Carl Sagan
blurb: A toolkit for distinguishing arguments that survive scrutiny from those that only sound like they do.

title: The Question of Global Warming
author: Freeman Dyson
blurb: Dyson argues climate models overweight atmospheric physics and underweight the carbon-vegetation exchange, proposes genetically engineered carbon-eating trees, and attacks climate science's drift toward dogma.

title: The Two Cultures
author: C. P. Snow
blurb: Literary intellectuals and physical scientists have become mutually unintelligible, and literary ignorance of the Second Law of Thermodynamics is treated as charming while scientific ignorance of Shakespeare is treated as barbarism.

title: The Power of the Powerless
author: Václav Havel
blurb: The greengrocer who puts "Workers of the world, unite!" in his window, and what happens when he stops.

title: A Cyborg Manifesto
author: Donna Haraway
blurb: The cyborg as a figure that refuses the boundaries between human and animal, organism and machine, physical and non-physical, and therefore refuses the origin myths feminism had been using.

title: The Case for Reparations
author: Ta-Nehisi Coates
blurb: Housing discrimination — redlining, and contract selling in Chicago's North Lawndale — as an ongoing, documentable theft of Black wealth.

title: Walking
author: Henry David Thoreau
blurb: Sauntering as a discipline, and the westward pull of the wild.

title: The American Crisis, No. I
author: Thomas Paine
blurb: "These are the times that try men's souls." Written during the retreat across New Jersey.

title: Uncanny Valley
author: Anna Wiener
blurb: A publishing assistant moves to San Francisco to work in customer support at a data-analytics startup and watches the industry's self-mythology from the bottom of it.

title: How Millennials Became The Burnout Generation
author: Anne Helen Petersen
blurb: Millennial burnout as a structural condition produced by precarity, credentialism, and always-on work.

title: The Case Against Travel
author: Agnes Callard
blurb: Tourism does not change you; travel's real function is chopping time into narrative segments to hide mortality. Argued through Emerson, Chesterton, and Pessoa.

title: The Case Against the Trauma Plot
author: Parul Sehgal
blurb: Contemporary fiction and television explain character almost exclusively through past injury, turning people into "a vivified DSM entry."

title: Why Women Aren't Welcome on the Internet
author: Amanda Hess
blurb: Hess documents her own stalker and the failure of police and platforms to treat threats as real, arguing harassment functions as a tax on women's ability to work online.

title: The Meaning of Serena Williams: On Tennis and Black Excellence
author: Claudia Rankine
blurb: Serena Williams's career as a case study in how Black excellence is policed, built on specific officiating incidents and press reactions.

title: The Really Big One
author: Kathryn Schulz
blurb: The Cascadia subduction zone is overdue for a magnitude 8–9 earthquake and tsunami the Pacific Northwest is not built for.

title: The Personal-Essay Boom Is Over
author: Jia Tolentino
blurb: Why the first-person internet essay economy collapsed, written from inside it — Tolentino had edited the Hairpin and Jezebel pipelines she is describing.

title: Joy
author: Zadie Smith
blurb: The distinction between pleasure, which is reliable and small, and joy, which is neither.

title: The Mother of All Questions
author: Rebecca Solnit
blurb: Framed around a public Q&A in which Solnit was asked about Virginia Woolf's childlessness.

title: The Communal Mind: The Internet and Me
author: Patricia Lockwood
blurb: What being permanently online does to attention, language, and moral perception, written in the fragmentary third person of a feed.

title: I Started the Media Men List
author: Moira Donegan
blurb: Why she made the anonymous "Shitty Media Men" spreadsheet, what it cost her, and the gap between informal warning systems and formal accountability.

title: The Secret Shame of Middle-Class Americans
author: Neal Gabler
blurb: A successful writer confesses he is financially insecure, and argues middle-class insolvency is widespread but hidden by shame.

title: Welcome to AirSpace
author: Kyle Chayka
blurb: How Airbnb, Instagram, Foursquare, and Yelp produce a globally identical café aesthetic — reclaimed wood, subway tile, Edison bulbs — that Chayka names "AirSpace."

title: Untangling Threads
author: Erin Kissane
blurb: Whether the fediverse should federate with Meta's Threads, argued from Meta's documented harms — the Rohingya genocide in Myanmar, harassment vectors, covert influence operations — rather than from abstract anti-big-tech principle.

title: Living Like Weasels
author: Annie Dillard
blurb: Dillard locks eyes with a weasel for sixty seconds at Hollins Pond and works out what it would mean to live from necessity rather than choice.

title: What White Publishers Won't Print
author: Zora Neale Hurston
blurb: Why the publishing industry will print Black suffering and Black exotica but not Black ordinariness.

title: Even Artichokes Have Doubts
author: Marina Keegan
blurb: Why a quarter of her graduating class was going into finance and consulting.

title: The Spandrels of San Marco and the Panglossian Paradigm
author: Stephen Jay Gould
blurb: Evolutionary biology's habit of assuming every trait is an adaptation, argued through the spandrels of San Marco, which exist because you cannot put a dome on arches without them.

title: On the Pursuit of the Ideal
author: Isaiah Berlin
blurb: Berlin's own late summary of value pluralism — that human goods are plural, genuinely conflicting, and not reducible to one another.

title: Shipping Out: On the (nearly lethal) comforts of a luxury cruise
author: David Foster Wallace
blurb: Seven nights on the MV *Zenith* in the Caribbean.

title: Ticket to the Fair
author: David Foster Wallace
blurb: The Illinois State Fair, attended as a native son sent back by a New York magazine.

title: Photography
author: Susan Sontag
blurb: Photographs as acquisition — of the thing photographed, and of a relation to it that feels like knowledge and is not.

title: The Perils of Pauline
author: Renata Adler
blurb: A review of Pauline Kael's *When the Lights Go Down* which concludes the book is "jarringly, piece by piece, line by line, and without interruption, worthless."

title: When We Dead Awaken: Writing as Re-Vision
author: Adrienne Rich
blurb: Re-vision — "entering an old text from a new critical direction" — as survival, traced through Rich's own move out of formalism.

title: Uses of the Erotic: The Erotic as Power
author: Audre Lorde
blurb: The erotic as a source of knowledge and power, distinguished from the pornographic.

title: The Ethics of Elfland
author: G. K. Chesterton
blurb: Fairy tales teach conditional joy — that the world is a gift held on terms — and that this is a better epistemology than the one that calls natural law necessity.

title: Twilight of Idols
author: Randolph Bourne
blurb: John Dewey's pragmatism had technique but no ends, and so was captured by the war.

title: A Free Man's Worship
author: Bertrand Russell
blurb: How to build a moral life on a universe that is indifferent and will end.

title: Mr. Bennett and Mrs. Brown
author: Virginia Woolf
blurb: Why the Edwardian novel's tools cannot capture an old woman in a railway carriage.

title: The Sahara of the Bozart
author: H. L. Mencken
blurb: The American South as a cultural desert. The title is Mencken's phonetic joke on *beaux arts*.

title: The Tipping Point
author: Malcolm Gladwell
blurb: Whether New York's crime collapse behaves like an epidemic reaching a threshold.

title: Black Body: Rereading James Baldwin's "Stranger in the Village"
author: Teju Cole
blurb: Cole goes to Leukerbad, the Swiss alpine village of Baldwin's 1953 essay, and rereads it against his own experience.

title: This Is What Black Burnout Feels Like
author: Tiana Clark
blurb: A response, published by the same outlet six days after Petersen's essay, on why the burnout framing does not account for Black women's labor.

title: The Egg
author: Andy Weir
blurb: A man dies in a car crash and a god explains that every human who ever lived is him, living each life in sequence. Kurzgesagt animated it in 2019 with Weir's permission; it is one of that channel's most-viewed videos, and the story has been fan-translated into 30+ languages. Logic built his 2017 album Everybody around the premise. No awards — it was never professionally published.

title: Story of Your Life
author: Ted Chiang
blurb: A linguist learns an alien written language whose simultaneous grammar restructures her perception of time. Won the Nebula for Best Novella and the Theodore Sturgeon Memorial Award (1999); Hugo-nominated. Adapted as Arrival (2016, Villeneuve), 8 Oscar nominations including Best Picture and Best Adapted Screenplay.

title: Exhalation
author: Ted Chiang
blurb: A mechanical scientist dissects his own brain while it runs and discovers his world is dying of air-pressure equalization. Won the 2009 Hugo for Best Short Story, the 2009 BSFA Award, and the 2009 Locus Award. The 2019 collection it names was a New York Times Notable Book and bestseller.

title: The Great Silence
author: Ted Chiang
blurb: A Puerto Rican parrot near the Arecibo Observatory observes that humans scan the sky for alien intelligence while the non-human intelligence beside them goes extinct.

title: The Lifecycle of Software Objects
author: Ted Chiang
blurb: Two employees of a failed virtual-pet startup spend twenty years raising AI "digients" as the platforms they live on go obsolete. Won the 2011 Hugo and Locus Awards for Best Novella. Standard reference in AI-alignment discussion for reframing AI development as long-horizon upbringing rather than engineering.

title: The Lottery
author: Shirley Jackson
blurb: A small town holds its annual civic ritual; the winner is stoned to death by her neighbours. The reader mail is the story: it drew the largest volume of mail The New Yorker had ever received for a work of fiction — roughly 10 letters a day that summer, and of some 300 Jackson counted, she said only 13 were kind. Subscriptions were cancelled. Banned in the Union of South Africa; adapted for NBC rad

title: Flowers for Algernon
author: Daniel Keyes
blurb: A man with an intellectual disability undergoes surgery that makes him a genius, then documents the reversal in his own journals. The short version won the 1960 Hugo; the novel tied for the Nebula for Best Novel with Delany's Babel-17, presented 1967. The 1968 film Charly won Cliff Robertson the Best Actor Oscar. 5M+ copies in 27 languages by 2004, and a perennial US banned-books list entry.

title: St. Lucy's Home for Girls Raised by Wolves
author: Karen Russell
blurb: Girls born to werewolf parents are civilised by nuns at a boarding school, told in five stages from a fictional handbook. The collection made Russell's career — NYT Notable Book 2006, feeding her selection to The New Yorker's "20 Under 40" (2010) and her 2013 MacArthur Fellowship. Now a fixture of the US high-school and AP English canon.

title: Interpreter of Maladies
author: Jhumpa Lahiri
blurb: An Indian tour guide who moonlights translating patients' symptoms for a doctor becomes the confessor of an Indian-American tourist, who tells him one of her sons is not her husband's. The story won an O. Henry Award (1999) and was selected for Best American Short Stories 1999 before the collection appeared; the 1999 collection won the 2000 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction and the PEN/Hemingway Award.

title: Harrison Bergeron
author: Kurt Vonnegut
blurb: In a future where handicapping devices enforce total equality, a superlative teenager tears his off on live television and is shot dead by the Handicapper General. Adapted three times, including the short 2081 (2009). Justice Antonin Scalia cited it in his dissent in PGA Tour, Inc. v. Martin (2001) — it is routinely invoked in equality-versus-excellence arguments, a use Vonnegut himself disputed.

title: Cathedral
author: Raymond Carver
blurb: A jealous narrator spends an evening with his wife's blind friend and ends up drawing a cathedral with the blind man's hand over his, eyes closed. Selected for Best American Short Stories 1982; the collection was a finalist for both the Pulitzer and the National Book Critics Circle Award. It marks the noted turn away from Carver's Lish-edited minimalism toward warmth — Carver said of the narrator,

title: What We Talk About When We Talk About Love
author: Raymond Carver
blurb: Two couples drink gin at a kitchen table and argue about what love is. The editing controversy is the reason to read it: Carver's original was titled "Beginners"; Gordon Lish cut roughly half, renamed characters, and deleted the elderly couple's backstory and eight closing paragraphs. Carver protested the "surgical amputation and transplant" — but the Antaeus text is already the Lish version, so t

title: A Good Man Is Hard to Find
author: Flannery O'Connor
blurb: A family's road-trip detour ends with an escaped convict, The Misfit, having them shot one by one. Her most anthologized story and the one she lectured on most — her essay "A Reasonable Use of the Unreasonable" exists chiefly to explain the grandmother's final gesture. Sufjan Stevens's 2004 song of the same name, on Seven Swans, is written from The Misfit's viewpoint.

title: The Library of Babel
author: Jorge Luis Borges
blurb: A librarian describes an infinite hexagonal library containing every possible 410-page book, and the sects and despairs this produces. The direct model for the labyrinth-library and blind Jorge of Burgos in Eco's The Name of the Rose. Spawned Jonathan Basile's libraryofbabel.info, a working algorithmic realisation.

title: The Garden of Forking Paths
author: Borges
blurb: A Chinese spy for Germany in the First World War visits a sinologist who has decoded his ancestor's novel as a labyrinth of branching times, then kills him to transmit a place name. Its Anthony Boucher translation in Ellery Queen's Mystery Magazine, August 1948, was the first Borges story ever published in English — he reached the anglophone world via a mystery pulp. The ancestor text of hypertext

title: Pierre Menard, Author of the Quixote
author: Borges
blurb: A mock obituary catalogues a minor French writer's attempt not to copy but to re-author, word for word, chapters of Don Quixote; the identical text is judged richer than Cervantes's. Routinely named the first work of postmodern fiction and a founding text of intertextuality; central to Arthur Danto's philosophy of art. Now the standard citation in arguments about machine-generated text.

title: Borges and I
author: Borges
blurb: The private man describes his public authorial double, who appropriates everything he does. The closing line — "I do not know which of us has written this page" — is among the most-quoted sentences in twentieth-century literature. Four major translators have taken it on, and the divergences between their versions are themselves a translation-studies case study.

title: The School
author: Donald Barthelme
blurb: A teacher lists everything his class has tried to raise — trees, herb gardens, gerbils, an orphan, parents — all of which died, and the children ask him about death. Literary Hub ran a close reading headlined "the best short story ever written"; it is a fixture of MFA escalation-and-comic-structure teaching. The Library of America chose it as the free public sample from its 2021 Collected Stories.

title: The Veldt
author: Ray Bradbury
blurb: Two children's virtual-reality nursery keeps rendering an African veldt with feeding lions; when the parents threaten to shut the house down, the children lock them in it. The standard early literary reference point for virtual reality, screen-parenting, and the smart home, cited constantly in tech criticism. Deadmau5's 2012 single "The Veldt" is explicitly based on it.

title: All Summer in a Day
author: Ray Bradbury
blurb: On Venus, where the sun appears for two hours every seven years, schoolchildren lock the one girl who remembers sunlight in a closet, and let her out after it has gone. The 1982 PBS WonderWorks adaptation softened the ending — the children bring Margot flowers — a change often used in classrooms to discuss adaptation. One of the most widely assigned middle-school stories in the US.

title: Nightfall
author: Isaac Asimov
blurb: On a planet with six suns, astronomers calculate that a once-in-2,049-years total eclipse is coming, and civilisation destroys itself when the stars appear. In 1968 the Science Fiction Writers of America voted it the best science fiction short story written before the Nebulas began, and enshrined it in The Science Fiction Hall of Fame, Volume One. Campbell paid a bonus rate of 1¼¢ a word — $166, m

title: The Overcoat
author: Nikolai Gogol
blurb: A despised copying clerk saves for a new overcoat, is robbed of it the night he first wears it, dies of grief after being humiliated by an official, and returns as a ghost stealing coats. Origin of the most-repeated line in Russian literary history — "We all came out from under Gogol's 'Overcoat'" — and of the Russian "little man" tradition. The object of Boris Eikhenbaum's "How Gogol's 'Overcoat'

title: Universal Love, Said The Cactus Person
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: A DMT trip, a cactus person, and a big green bat with many faces; the narrator demands they factor a large number as proof they are real, they refuse and talk about universal love, and after he wakes they casually reveal they knew the factorization all along. Hit MetaFilter within a day of posting. Canonical rationalist-blogosphere text — "the cactus person" is in-group shorthand — with recurring

title: Cat Person
author: Kristen Roupenian
blurb: A 20-year-old student texts her way into a date and into sex she does not want with a 34-year-old man, then has a friend break it off; he texts her the word "whore." The New Yorker's most-read fiction of 2017 and one of its most-read pieces of any kind that year; it drove a reported $1.2M Scout Press deal for You Know You Want This. Then Alexis Nowicki, "'Cat Person' and Me," Slate, July 8, 2021 —

title: The War Prayer
author: Mark Twain
blurb: An aged stranger interrupts a patriotic church service to spell out the unspoken second half of the congregation's prayer for victory — the enemy's children starving, their homes in ruins — and is dismissed as a lunatic. Citation flag: the widely repeated Harper's Monthly, November 1916 first-publication claim is wrong. Written against the Philippine-American War and revived as a protest document

title: A Christmas Carol
author: Charles Dickens
blurb: The 6,000-copy first printing sold out by Christmas Eve and thirteen editions followed by the end of 1844; it has never been out of print. It popularized "Merry Christmas" and "Bah! Humbug!", and "Scrooge" was admitted to the OED as a common noun in 1982.

title: This Is Water
author: David Foster Wallace
blurb: Liberal-arts education as training in choosing what to pay attention to, against the default setting of unconscious self-centeredness.

title: The Weight of Glory
author: C. S. Lewis
blurb: Desire (Sehnsucht) as evidence of a destiny beyond the world, and the resulting weight of the destinies of the people beside you. Source of the most-quoted sentence in Lewis's nonfiction — "half-hearted creatures fooling about with drink and sex and ambition when infinite joy is offered us… far too easily pleased" — and of "you have never talked to a mere mortal."

title: Learning in War-Time
author: C. S. Lewis
blurb: Why scholarship and culture are legitimate rather than frivolous while a war is on — the human condition has always been lived on the edge of a precipice. It became the most-cited historical text during COVID-19 for justifying continued academic work in a crisis, and its claim that war "creates no absolutely new situation" is a standard rebuttal in arguments about the humanities' relevance.

title: Existentialism Is a Humanism
author: Jean-Paul Sartre
blurb: Defends existentialism against charges of quietism and despair — existence precedes essence, and man is condemned to be free.

title: A Room of One's Own
author: Virginia Woolf
blurb: Money and privacy as the material preconditions of women's writing, argued through the invented figure of Shakespeare's sister Judith.

title: How Should One Read a Book?
author: Virginia Woolf
blurb: The reader's only duty is to follow her own instincts — first as the author's accomplice, then as judge. Source of the closing image of God telling readers at Judgment Day, "we have nothing to give them here… they have loved reading." A permanent fixture of introductory literature and library-science syllabi.

title: National Book Foundation Medal acceptance
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
blurb: A defense of imaginative literature and of writers as "realists of a larger reality," and an attack on publishers who treat books as commodities. Words Are My Matter, the collection built around it, won the 2017 Hugo for Best Related Work. Reprinted within days by the Poetry Foundation, SFWA, and the Guardian; recirculated at scale on her death in January 2018. The most-quoted line: "We live in ca

title: Nobel Lecture
author: Toni Morrison
blurb: Opens "Once upon a time there was an old woman. Blind but wise." Children bring her a bird and ask whether it is living or dead; she says she does not know, but "what I do know is that it is in your hands." The bird is language; the old woman is a practiced writer. Morrison was the first Black woman to win the Nobel in Literature, and this is the definitive statement of her poetics. "We die. That

title: Nobel banquet speech
author: William Faulkner
blurb: Under the shadow of the atomic bomb, the writer's only worthy subject is "the problems of the human heart in conflict with itself." Textual flag: Faulkner revised it for The Faulkner Reader (1954), and the version circulating today — including on the Nobel site — carries those changes; it is not verbatim what he said. "I decline to accept the end of man… he will not merely endure: he will prevail"

title: Nobel Lecture
author: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn
blurb: How the text reached the West is itself the story: he photographed the manuscript and, at a clandestine meeting at the Belorussian railway station in late April 1972, handed nine negatives to Swedish journalist Stig Fredrikson, who cut them into strips, wrapped them in plastic, hid the roll in an empty headache-tablet tube, concealed that in a transistor radio's battery compartment, and carried it

title: Make Good Art
author: Neil Gaiman
blurb: How to survive a freelance creative career: make mistakes, ignore the rules you don't know, and when things go wrong, make good art. Went viral within days and became the template for the commencement-speech-as-shareable-object genre of the early 2010s; the Chip Kidd book turned it into a design object. "Make good art" is on posters, tattoos, and studio walls, and TED-Ed built a lesson around it.

title: Convocation address (Congratulations, by the way)
author: George Saunders
blurb: His chief regret is not his failures but his "failures of kindness," and kindness is a skill that can be deliberately increased. Among the most-shared items the Times published in 2013 — the book deal was announced six days after the blog post. It established Saunders as a public moral voice outside fiction.

title: We Should All Be Feminists
author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
blurb: A defence of the word "feminist," argued from Nigerian and American experience, against the claim that it is un-African, anti-male, or unnecessary. Beyoncé sampled the talk directly on "\\\Flawless" (BEYONCÉ, surprise-released December 13, 2013), with Adichie credited — which moved the argument from a TEDx stage to global pop radio and onto a 2017 Dior T-shirt. In December 2015 the Swedish Women's

title: The Danger of a Single Story
author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
blurb: How a single repeated narrative about a people flattens them, and what that does to both the told-about and the teller. Among the most widely assigned texts in the world's first-year writing and world-literature curricula.

title: The Transformation of Silence into Language and Action
author: Audre Lorde
blurb: Written after a breast-cancer scare: silence bought no safety, and speech is a survival act rather than a luxury. "Your silence will not protect you" became a standing slogan of feminist, queer, and anti-racist organizing, and supplied the title of the 2017 UK Lorde collection.

title: Madness, Rack, and Honey / On Fear
author: Mary Ruefle
blurb: "On Fear" traces fear as the engine of poetic composition. The title lecture argues poetry "disequips you for the requirements of life."

title: An Image of Africa: Racism in Conrad's Heart of Darkness
author: Chinua Achebe
blurb: It single-handedly reframed the teaching of Heart of Darkness worldwide — no serious edition or syllabus now presents Conrad without Achebe's rebuttal. The founding document of postcolonial critique's confrontation with the Western canon, predating and shaping Said's Culture and Imperialism.

title: The Fringe Benefits of Failure, and the Importance of Imagination
author: J. K. Rowling
blurb: The most widely circulated speech ever given on failure as a professional asset. Harvard President Drew Faust called it the most moving and memorable commencement address she had seen. The seven-year gap between delivery and book is the measure of how durable demand for the printed text was.

title: Bad Feminist
author: Roxane Gay
blurb: Gay's refusal of "essential feminism" and her account of her own contradictions. The collection was a New York Times bestseller that made her a mainstream cultural critic, and "bad feminist" entered general usage as shorthand for imperfect, non-doctrinaire feminism.

title: The Careless Language of Sexual Violence
author: Roxane Gay
blurb: A critique of the New York Times's coverage of the gang rape of an 11-year-old in Cleveland, Texas. The piece that first built Gay's national readership, years before the books, and now a standard media-ethics teaching text.

title: The Laugh of the Medusa
author: Hélène Cixous
blurb: Women must write themselves and their bodies into a language built to exclude them. The founding statement of écriture féminine, and one of the most-assigned essays in Anglophone feminist theory.

title: The Morals of Chess
author: Benjamin Franklin
blurb: Chess as moral training in foresight, caution, and sportsmanship. Generally regarded as the first essay on chess published in America; reprinted at least a dozen times before 1800 and translated into French, German, and Russian — the most widely reprinted product of Franklin's Passy press.

title: Against "National Poetry Month" As Such
author: Charles Bernstein
blurb: National Poetry Month promotes sanitized, accessible verse and suppresses innovative poetry. The canonical dissent against NPM, recirculated every April since 1999; its proposed "International Anti-Poetry Month" became a running joke in avant-garde poetry circles.

title: Putinism: The Ideology
author: Anne Applebaum
blurb: Putinism as a coherent ideology rooted in KGB institutional culture, with authority vested in personalities rather than institutions. An early, pre-Crimea argument that Putinism was ideological rather than merely kleptocratic, much cited after 2014. Paired with an LSE public lecture still on their site.

title: Everything Is Fiction — author correction
author: Keith Ridgway
blurb: "I don't know how to write" — narrative as the mechanism by which everyone constructs their own life. Went viral among writers in 2012 and is still an anthologized craft essay; it drove Anglophone attention to Hawthorn & Child, the novel that made Ridgway a cult figure.

title: Letter to His Father (Brief an den Vater)
author: Franz Kafka
blurb: An itemized indictment of paternal domination and its effect on his writing, his attempts at marriage, and his self. The single most-quoted biographical key to Kafka's fiction and the origin of the modern letter-to-a-parent genre. The manuscript was acquired by the Deutsches Literaturarchiv Marbach, announced 2025.

title: On Noise
author: Seneca
blurb: Seneca lodges above a bathhouse and catalogues every noise coming through the floor — grunting weightlifters, the armpit-hair plucker's clients shrieking — then argues that the real obstacle to study is internal, not acoustic. Your second Seneca after #65.

title: Here Is New York
author: E. B. White
blurb: A block-by-block meditation on New York as three cities — commuter, native, settler — and on the privacy and loneliness it confers.

title: Good-bye to Forty-Eighth Street
author: E. B. White
blurb: White tries to disperse the contents of his Turtle Bay apartment before leaving New York for Maine, and finds the objects will not go.

title: The Ring of Time
author: E. B. White
blurb: A young circus rider rehearses bareback in a Florida practice ring while White tries to fix the enchantment of the moment on paper.

title: Walden
author: E. B. White
blurb: A letter dictated to Henry Thoreau reporting on a 1939 motor trip to Walden Pond, complete with an itemized expense list.

title: Freedom
author: E. B. White
blurb: Written as France fell, it defines freedom as a private, physically felt possession rather than a political abstraction.

title: Obituary (for Daisy)
author: E. B. White
blurb: A mock-formal obituary for White's Scottish terrier, killed by a Yellow Cab on University Place.

title: Letter to Mr. Nadeau
author: E. B. White
blurb: A reply to a stranger who wrote that he had lost faith in humanity's future.

title: Letter to the Xerox Corporation
author: E. B. White
blurb: Why Xerox's underwriting of a magazine article, however hands-off, damages press independence.

title: Slouching Towards Bethlehem
author: Joan Didion
blurb: Reportage from the Haight-Ashbury in spring 1967, ending with a five-year-old on acid.

title: Some Dreamers of the Golden Dream
author: Joan Didion
blurb: The Lucille Miller murder trial in San Bernardino, told as a parable of the valley itself.

title: On Morality
author: Joan Didion
blurb: Written from a Death Valley motel on assignment, it reduces morality to the wagon-train loyalty of not leaving the dead unburied.

title: On Going Home
author: Joan Didion
blurb: Didion returns to her family's Central Valley house for her daughter's first birthday and finds she cannot translate between her two homes.

title: Why I Write
author: Joan Didion
blurb: She writes to find out what she thinks, and grammar and pictures in the mind, not ideas, dictate her sentences.

title: In Bed
author: Joan Didion
blurb: Three or four days a month lost to migraine, and the shame of an illness with no visible cause.

title: Insider Baseball
author: Joan Didion
blurb: The 1988 Dukakis campaign as a closed performance staged by operatives and reporters for each other.

title: Sentimental Journeys
author: Joan Didion
blurb: The Central Park jogger case read as a narrative New York told itself to avoid discussing class and money.

title: The Modern Essay
author: Virginia Woolf
blurb: A review of Ernest Rhys's anthology that turns into Woolf's theory of what the essay form must do.

title: Montaigne
author: Virginia Woolf
blurb: On Montaigne's attempt to draw himself with a pen, and the impossibility of communicating a soul.

title: On Not Knowing Greek
author: Virginia Woolf
blurb: Why the Greek of Aeschylus and Sophocles stays permanently out of reach of English readers, and why we keep returning to it.

title: The Common Reader
author: Virginia Woolf
blurb: A one-page defence, taken from Johnson's Life of Gray, of the reader who reads for pleasure rather than to instruct.

title: Professions for Women
author: Virginia Woolf
blurb: Woolf describes having to murder "the Angel in the House" before she could review a book honestly.

title: Craftsmanship
author: Virginia Woolf
blurb: Writing is not a craft, because words refuse to be pinned to single useful meanings.

title: Thoughts on Peace in an Air Raid
author: Virginia Woolf
blurb: Written under German bombers over Sussex: women must help men kill the "subconscious Hitlerism" of the desire to dominate.

title: Three Guineas
author: Virginia Woolf
blurb: Answering a letter asking how war may be prevented, Woolf links fascism abroad to patriarchy in English education, professions and the family.

title: Such, Such Were the Joys
author: George Orwell
blurb: St Cyprian's preparatory school: bed-wetting, beatings, snobbery, and the child's conviction of being irredeemably bad.

title: Reflections on Gandhi
author: George Orwell
blurb: A sceptical assessment of Gandhi's sainthood, asking whether non-violence could have worked against a totalitarian state.

title: Notes on Nationalism
author: George Orwell
blurb: Distinguishes patriotism from nationalism — the habit of identifying with a unit and refusing all evidence against it.

title: Charles Dickens
author: George Orwell
blurb: A long political reading of Dickens as a moralist who wanted men to behave better rather than institutions to change.

title: Books v. Cigarettes
author: George Orwell
blurb: Orwell audits his own 442-book library to prove reading costs less than tobacco or the cinema.

title: Confessions of a Book Reviewer
author: George Orwell
blurb: A portrait of the reviewer in a cold dressing-gown, inventing enthusiasm for books that deserve none.

title: Decline of the English Murder
author: George Orwell
blurb: Why the respectable domestic poisoning of 1850–1925 satisfied the English public more than the 1944 Cleft Chin Murder.

title: A Nice Cup of Tea
author: George Orwell
blurb: Eleven non-negotiable rules for making tea, including milk after and never sugar.

title: Bookshop Memories
author: George Orwell
blurb: A year behind the counter at Booklovers' Corner, Hampstead, and the customers who cured him of wanting to own a bookshop.

title: Everybody's Protest Novel
author: James Baldwin
blurb: Attacks Uncle Tom's Cabin and, at the end, Native Son, as sentimental protest fiction that denies its subjects' humanity.

title: Many Thousands Gone
author: James Baldwin
blurb: Bigger Thomas is a white American fantasy, and "the Negro in America" exists only as a national myth.

title: Equal in Paris
author: James Baldwin
blurb: Eight days in a French prison in December 1949 over a stolen hotel bedsheet, and the laughter of the courtroom.

title: The Discovery of What It Means to Be an American
author: James Baldwin
blurb: Exile in Europe is what taught him he was an American writer rather than a Negro writer.

title: My Dungeon Shook
author: James Baldwin
blurb: Baldwin tells his fifteen-year-old namesake nephew that white Americans, not he, are the ones trapped in a history they do not understand.

title: A Talk to Teachers
author: James Baldwin
blurb: Addressed to New York schoolteachers on what an honest education would have to tell a Black child about America.

title: If Black English Isn't a Language, Then Tell Me, What Is?
author: James Baldwin
blurb: Black English is a language forged under conditions no other Americans faced, and schools punish children for speaking it.

title: Tense Present: Democracy, English, and the Wars over Usage
author: David Foster Wallace
blurb: A review of Bryan Garner's usage dictionary that becomes an argument about descriptivism, prescriptivism, and the class politics of Standard Written English.

title: The Nature of the Fun
author: David Foster Wallace
blurb: Why novelists keep writing once the vanity motive dies, built on DeLillo's image of the book as a deformed infant.

title: Deciderization 2007 — A Special Report
author: David Foster Wallace
blurb: His guest-editor introduction on choosing twenty-two essays while drowning in information.

title: Host
author: David Foster Wallace
blurb: A reported profile of Los Angeles conservative talk-radio host John Ziegler and the economics of outrage radio.

title: Fascinating Fascism
author: Susan Sontag
blurb: Leni Riefenstahl's Nuba photo book and a book of SS regalia, used to define a persistent fascist aesthetic.

title: The Aesthetics of Silence
author: Susan Sontag
blurb: Twenty numbered sections on silence, negation and renunciation as the modern artist's spiritual programme.

title: Illness as Metaphor
author: Susan Sontag
blurb: Tuberculosis and cancer are smothered in punitive metaphor, and the healthiest way to be ill is to resist it.

title: Godot Comes to Sarajevo
author: Susan Sontag
blurb: First-person account of directing Waiting for Godot by candlelight in besieged Sarajevo.

title: The Imagination of Disaster
author: Susan Sontag
blurb: Science-fiction disaster films read as collective rehearsal for nuclear annihilation and mass death.

title: Seeing
author: Annie Dillard
blurb: Hidden pennies, cataract patients given sight, and the difference between looking and letting go into seeing.

title: Transfiguration (The Death of a Moth)
author: Annie Dillard
blurb: A moth burning in a candle flame as a figure for the writer consumed by her vocation.

title: Singing with the Fundamentalists
author: Annie Dillard
blurb: Dillard joins evangelical students singing on a West Coast campus plaza and refuses the expected condescension.

title: The Wreck of Time
author: Annie Dillard
blurb: Numbers — birth rates, death tolls, grains of sand — set against the question of whether one life can matter.

title: Write Till You Drop
author: Annie Dillard
blurb: Spend everything on the page now rather than hoarding material.

title: The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
blurb: A perfect city whose happiness depends on one child kept in permanent misery.

title: A Left-Handed Commencement Address
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
blurb: Tells graduating women to refuse the man's-world success script and speak in their own language.

title: The Operating Instructions
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
blurb: Imagination is a survival tool and literature the operating manual for being human.

title: A Rant About Technology
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
blurb: Rejects the equation of technology with high tech — a clay pot and a spindle are technology too.

title: Some Assumptions About Fantasy
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
blurb: Dismantles three assumptions about fantasy: white characters, pseudo-medieval Europe, and simple good against evil.

title: The Loneliness of Donald Trump
author: Rebecca Solnit
blurb: Trump as a fairy-tale figure destroyed by having every wish granted and never being told the truth.

title: Whose Story (and Country) Is This?
author: Rebecca Solnit
blurb: The myth of a "real America," and whose suffering the culture agrees to find interesting.

title: Diary: In the Day of the Postman
author: Rebecca Solnit
blurb: How email and smartphones destroyed the texture of unhurried attention and correspondence.

title: From Lying to Leering
author: Rebecca Solnit
blurb: Trump's misogyny, the Access Hollywood tape, and the retraumatising effect of the 2016 debates.

title: Speaking in Tongues
author: Zadie Smith
blurb: Losing her Willesden voice at Cambridge, Eliza Doolittle, and Obama's multiple voices as a model of self.

title: Two Paths for the Novel
author: Zadie Smith
blurb: O'Neill's Netherland against McCarthy's Remainder as rival futures for fiction.

title: Generation Why?
author: Zadie Smith
blurb: The Social Network and Facebook as software that shrinks the person to fit the database.

title: Fascinated to Presume: In Defense of Fiction
author: Zadie Smith
blurb: Defends the novelist's presumption of entering other lives against identity-bounded arguments about who may write whom.

title: The Gig Economy Celebrates Working Yourself to Death
author: Jia Tolentino
blurb: Lyft's cheerful blog post about a driver who kept taking fares while in labour.
